chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazee' from Muhammad ibn Udhafir from Uqbah from Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Ja'far (peace be upon him) was asked about the Takbir (saying Allahu Akbar) during funeral prayers, so he said: 'That is up to the family of the deceased; whatever they wish, they may say Takbir.' It was said to him: 'Indeed, they say Takbir four times.' He said: 'That is up to them.'

Then he said: 'Has it not reached you that a man for whom Ali (peace be upon him) prayed, he said Takbir over him five times, until he prayed over him five prayers, saying five Takbirs in each prayer.'

Then he said: 'Indeed, he was Badri, Aqabi, Uhudi, and he was among the twelve leaders whom the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) chose, so he had five virtues.' So he prayed over him for each virtue a prayer.

And it is possible that what he (peace be upon him) meant by 'four' is what is recited between the Takbirs, because the fifth Takbir is not followed by a supplication, but rather one turns away from the funeral with it. This is indicated by what was narrated.

key_terms.أُحُدِيٌّ: One who participated in the Battle of Uhud
key_terms.التَّكْبِير: Saying 'Allahu Akbar' (God is Greater), a ritual utterance in prayer
key_terms.النُّقَبَاء: The leaders / chiefs (specifically the twelve chosen by the Prophet)
key_terms.بَدْرِيٌّ: One who participated in the Battle of Badr
key_terms.عَقَبِيٌّ: One who participated in the Battle of Uhud or the subsequent expedition (contextually linked to early Islamic battles)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the number of Takbirs in Shia funeral prayer and what is the example of Imam Ali's prayer?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that the number of Takbirs in the funeral prayer is not rigidly fixed but allows for flexibility based on the deceased's status, citing Imam Ali’s (peace be upon him) unique practice of offering five distinct prayers with five Takbirs each to honor a companion’s five specific virtues (Badri, Aqabi, Uhudi, and being one of the twelve chosen leaders). This narration highlights the Shia scholarly view that the 'four' Takbirs commonly practiced may refer to the recitations between them, with the fifth serving as the concluding turn, thereby distinguishing the ritual structure from the number of invocations. The hadith underscores the theological principle that the prayer can be adapted to reflect the spiritual rank and specific merits of the deceased, a concept rooted in the flexibility of Sunnah as interpreted by the Ahl al-Bayt.
